# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Gets Upstairs

Turn on a faucet on the 40th floor of an apartment building and water comes out, seemingly as easily as it does in a basement laundry room. Behind this everyday miracle lies a carefully engineered system that fights gravity the entire way. Let's trace the journey, using a concrete example: a reservoir sitting in hills above a fictional city, feeding a 40-story apartment tower we'll call the Meridian.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation as Pressure

The core principle is deceptively simple: water pressure in a municipal system is largely a function of elevation. Every 2.31 feet of vertical drop generates about 1 pound per square inch (PSI) of pressure. Engineers call this "head" — the height of a water column above a given point.

Imagine our reservoir sits at 500 feet above sea level, in hills three miles from the city. The Meridian's street-level connection sits at 100 feet elevation. That 400-foot difference means the water arriving at the building's base already carries roughly 173 PSI of pressure — far more than the 50–80 PSI typically desired at a fixture. Gravity, in other words, is doing the pumping for free
